Fujisawa, Amarasingham, Harrison and Buzsaki (2008) on CRCNS pfc-2¶

Paper: Fujisawa S, Amarasingham A, Harrison MT, Buzsaki G. Behavior-dependent short-term assembly dynamics in the medial prefrontal cortex. Nature Neuroscience 11:823-833 (2008), doi:10.1038/nn.2134. The claims file, claims/crcns-pfc-2/10.1038-nn.2134.yaml, was written from the version of record with its supplement.

Dataset: CRCNS pfc-2, doi:10.6080/K01V5BWK (dataset crcns:pfc-2/unversioned). CRCNS data sets are not versioned (docs/archives.md), so the version pinned is unversioned: the files as they are in the bucket crcnsarchive under pfc-2/live/, the only published copy, documented by the data description version 0.7 (2021). The MD5 sums of the files read, from the data set's checksums.md5, are printed below and compared with the bytes read, so that a later change is detectable. Files read: data/behaviors.zip, data/EE0708/EE188_Behavior.mat, data/EE0708/EE188_Behavior_PFC.mat, and, from data/EE0708/EE.188.tar.gz, the member EE188_example.mat, the list of members, and channels 97 and 98 (the nose-poke sensors) of the member EE.188.eeg.

Revision after the first verification round: the global band of the jitter test follows the Methods' stepping procedure (G-b) for every connection claim, with the first version's 1% on each side (G-a) as a variant; the spike-order test takes its P from both tails of the permutation distribution; the nose-poke window is the sensor-detected pokes; the lateral coordinate of the path is y; task performance is tested on EE188 from the sensor channels; thinning counts only flattened repetitions; and checks the verifier asked for are added (detector false positives on shifted trains, the cells' rates against the 1 Hz rule, the tar's members, the maze geometry, presynaptic-only jitter).

Claims (outcomes are in the attempt record and the summary at the end).

with fsspec.open(pfc2.BASE + "behaviors.zip", block_size=2**22) as f:

Data check¶

The data set holds 13 working memory sessions of three rats (EE, FF, GG). The paper recorded four rats; Supplementary Figure 1 names them E, G and H (layer 2/3) and F (layer 5). The data set's rats EE, FF and GG are taken to be the paper's E, F and G (an assumption: the names match and the data description names EE.188 as the session of Figures 2a and 3d, which is layer 2/3); rat H is not in the data set. So FF is the layer 5 rat.

The trial table, SessionNP, lists correct trials only (data description, page 2); error trials can be found only from the nose-poke sensor channels of a session's .eeg file, read here for EE188 (task-performance). Above: every spike with a trial label falls in that trial's interval from the first nose-poke to the trial end (so the spikes' trials, and their positions near 0, include the nose-poke, which the description's trial start, the end of the nose-poke, does not); the spike positions agree with the position file; the spike times in 20 kHz samples, converted to seconds, end with the position file. The CellsInfo type column is described as pyramidal (1), interneuron (2) or unknown (3): in the 12 sessions of behaviors.zip and in EE188_Behavior_PFC.mat no cell is unknown, while EE188_example.mat has 33, 15 and 69.

Clock check. Every analysis here uses the spike times and the trial table, and the position file for the claims on paths, speed and synchrony. To show they share one clock, the trial side (left or right) is decoded from the population spike counts in the 2 s after each trial start in the 3 s before each trial end, in the side arm (nearest centroid, leave one out), once with the true trial times and once with the times shifted by 30 s. The position file is checked by the agreement of spikeX with the file's position at the spike time (above), and by decoding the side from the position file's x coordinate 2 to 4 s after the trial start (end of the nose-poke) against the same shift.

In [4]:
def loo_centroid(X, y):
    X = (X - X.mean(0)) / (X.std(0) + 1e-9)
    hit = 0
    for i in range(len(y)):
        m = np.ones(len(y), bool)
        m[i] = False
        c1, c0 = X[m & y].mean(0), X[m & ~y].mean(0)
        hit += (np.sum((X[i] - c1) ** 2) < np.sum((X[i] - c0) ** 2)) == y[i]
    return hit / len(y)


def clock_check(s, shift):
    st = s.NP[:, 1] + shift
    en = s.NP[:, 2] + shift
    X = np.zeros((s.ntrials, s.n))
    for k, t0 in enumerate(en):
        a, b = np.searchsorted(s.t, [t0 - 3.0, t0])
        X[k] = np.bincount(s.u[a:b], minlength=s.n)
    acc_sp = loo_centroid(X, s.left)
    fr = ((st[:, None] + np.linspace(2, 4, 9)) * pfc2.WHL_RATE).astype(int)
    fr = np.clip(fr, 0, len(s.whl) - 1)
    acc_x = loo_centroid(s.whl[fr, 0], s.left)
    return acc_sp, acc_x

for k, s in S.items():

    a1, x1 = clock_check(s, 30.0)

unit-count¶

A total of 633 well-isolated units were recorded from anterior cingulate and dorsal prelimbic cortex in four rats.

The criterion: the number of distinct sorted PFC units over all working memory task recordings, counted per recording day. The cells of each session are those of its CellsInfo (for EE188, the 117 of EE188_example.mat; the 105 of EE188_Behavior_PFC.mat are a variant). The data set holds three of the paper's four rats. The files also list every cluster of the day's sorting (spikeph), shown as a variant. The data description defines Cells as the units "whose max firing rates are more than 1 Hz in the trials" (page 2); the files hold no variable of that name, so each cell's largest rate over the tenths of the maze is printed to show which selection the files keep.

# Which selection are the files' cells? The data description defines Cells as "the neuron # whose
# max firing rates are more than 1 Hz in the trials" (page 2); the files hold no variable of that
# name. Each cell's largest rate over the tenths of the maze on left and right trials (spikes over
# time spent, from the position file) is computed for every cell kept, and for the 12 cells of
# EE188_example.mat that EE188_Behavior_PFC.mat leaves out.
def max_trial_rate(s, cells):
    w = s.whl
    side_f = w[:, 4].astype(int)
    d = w[:, 6]
    inf = d > 0
    tenth_f = np.minimum(((d[inf] - 1) * 10).astype(int), 9)
    occ = np.zeros((3, 10))
    np.add.at(occ, (side_f[inf], tenth_f), 1 / pfc2.WHL_RATE)
    m = s.intrial
    side_s = np.where(s.left[np.maximum(s.trial, 0)], 2, 1)[m]
    tenth_s = np.minimum((s.x[m] * 10).astype(int), 9)
    cnt = np.zeros((s.n, 3, 10))
    np.add.at(cnt, (s.u[m], side_s, tenth_s), 1)
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
        rate = np.where(occ[None, 1:] > 0, cnt[:, 1:] / occ[None, 1:], 0)
    return rate.reshape(s.n, -1).max(1)[cells]


for k, s in S.items():
    r = max_trial_rate(s, np.arange(s.n))
    extra = ""
    if k == "EE188":
        out = ~np.isin(s.cells, c105)
        extra = (f"; the 12 cells not in EE188_Behavior_PFC.mat: {np.sort(r[out]).round(2).tolist()} Hz, of the other 105 "
                 f"{np.sum(r[~out] > 1)} above 1 Hz")
    print(f"{k}: cells with a largest trial rate above 1 Hz {np.sum(r > 1)} of {s.n} (lowest {r.min():.2f} Hz){extra}")

Result: partially reproduced. The 13 working memory sessions of three rats hold 627 cells (615 with EE188 counted as the 105 cells of its Behavior_PFC file), within 10% of the paper's 633, but the paper counts four rats and rat H is not in the data set. The cells are a selection of the 1,495 clusters the files list: by the largest rate over the tenths of the maze, 0 to 10 cells per session fall below 1 Hz (10 of 117 in EE188, 5 of the 12 EE188 cells that EE188_Behavior_PFC.mat leaves out), which is consistent with the data description's 1 Hz rule for Cells without showing it. The match in number therefore does not show that the same units are counted.

task-performance¶

The rats performed the task with a mean of 91.9% correct choices during the recording sessions.

The trial table, SessionNP, holds correct trials only (data description, page 2: "Only correct trials are listed"), so the claims file's test cannot be run from it. The session tar of EE188, streamed for EE188_example.mat, also holds the session's .eeg file with the two nose-poke sensor channels (97, right trials; 98, left trials; data description, page 1), and the position file covers the whole session. Every trial, error trials included, can therefore be found in EE188: a trial is the run of pokes since the last arm-end visit, its type the channel poked, and its choice the arm end reached next (within 60 pixels of the median end position of the table's correct trials of that side; 40 and 80 pixels as variants). Correct when the arm matches the channel. The other 12 sessions' sensor channels are in their own tars (about 2 GB each, read only as a stream), not read here for time, so the claim is tested on one session of 13. The members of the EE188 tar are listed first.

s = S["EE188"]
sens = raw["EE188 nose-poke sensors"]
PK = {1: pfc2.poke_intervals(sens[:, 0]), 2: pfc2.poke_intervals(sens[:, 1])}
w = s.whl
t_f = np.arange(len(w)) / pfc2.WHL_RATE
ok_f = w[:, 0] > 0
two = w[:, 2] > 0
px = np.where(two, (w[:, 0] + w[:, 2]) / 2, w[:, 0])
py = np.where(two, (w[:, 1] + w[:, 3]) / 2, w[:, 1])
ends = {}
for side in (1, 2):
    f = np.minimum((s.NP[s.NP[:, 3] == side, 2] * pfc2.WHL_RATE).astype(int), len(w) - 1)
    ends[side] = (np.median(px[f]), np.median(py[f]))
print(f"arm ends (median position at the end of the table's correct trials): right {np.round(ends[1], 0)}, left "
      f"{np.round(ends[2], 0)} pixels; sensor pokes: right channel {len(PK[1])}, left channel {len(PK[2])}")


def all_trials(radius):
    ev = []
    for sd in (1, 2):
        near = ok_f & (np.hypot(px - ends[sd][0], py - ends[sd][1]) < radius)
        ev += [(t_f[i], "arm", sd, t_f[i]) for i in np.flatnonzero(np.diff(near.astype(int), prepend=0) == 1)]
        ev += [(a, "poke", sd, b) for a, b in PK[sd]]
    ev.sort()
    out, pending = [], []
    for t, kind, sd, t_end in ev:
        if kind == "poke":
            pending.append((t, sd, t_end))
        elif pending:
            # first poke, channels poked, arm reached, arrival, end of the last poke, number of pokes
            out.append((pending[0][0], {c for _, c, _ in pending}, sd, t, pending[-1][2], len(pending)))
            pending = []
    return out


PERF = {}
for radius in (60, 40, 80):
    tr = all_trials(radius)
    mixed = sum(len(x[1]) > 1 for x in tr)
    corr = [x for x in tr if len(x[1]) == 1 and min(x[1]) == x[2]]
    err = [x for x in tr if len(x[1]) == 1 and min(x[1]) != x[2]]
    matched = sum(any(abs(x[0] - r[0]) < 0.05 and x in corr and min(x[1]) == r[3] for x in tr) for r in s.NP)
    PERF[radius] = 100 * len(corr) / (len(corr) + len(err))
    print(f"radius {radius} px: {len(tr)} trials, {len(corr)} correct, {len(err)} error, {mixed} with pokes on both channels; "
          f"table rows matched to a detected correct trial of the same side by the first poke (within 50 ms): {matched} of "
          f"{len(s.NP)}; performance {PERF[radius]:.1f}% (within 91.9 +- 9.19: {abs(PERF[radius] - 91.9) <= 9.19})")
    if radius == 60:
        print(f"    table trials, first poke to trial end: {(s.NP[:, 2] - s.NP[:, 0]).min():.1f} to {(s.NP[:, 2] - s.NP[:, 0]).max():.1f} s")
        for x in tr:

                                  for x in inn))

In EE188, the one session whose sensor channels are read, 45 of 46 trials are correct (97.8%; 95.8% with an 80 pixel radius), within 91.9 +- 9.19; 41 of the table's 42 correct trials are found as correct trials of the same side, and the one left over (first poke 1133.5 s) lies within a detected correct trial of the same side whose first poke is 3.5 s earlier. One of these correct trials (first poke 2245.1 s) reaches the arm 25.9 s after its first poke, within the 9.0 to 36.1 s of the table's trials; the other two (822.9 and 2370.7 s) reach it 199.8 and 259.9 s after the first poke, 193.4 and 176.9 s after the last, longer than any table trial, so they may not be ordinary trials. Without these two, 43 of 44 trials are correct (97.7%). The other 12 sessions are not tested.

Firing rates along the maze¶

Per cell, the per-trial PSTH: the normalised positions (spikeX) of the spikes between the trial start (end of the nose-poke) and the trial end, as the data description defines them (page 2, SessionNP; the spikes' own trial labels also cover the nose-poke, where the rat stays at position 0 for up to 30 s), smoothed with the Gaussian kernel of bandwidth 0.05 (Methods), so that a condition's PSTH is the mean over its trials. Left and right PSTHs are compared by the Methods' permutation test with global bands (1,000 permutations, level 0.05, Figure 1c legend). Only correct trials are in the data set, so the claims file's reading T-a (correct trials only) is the one run; T-b (all trials) cannot be.

def session_psths(s):
    return np.array([pfc2.smooth(s.trial_hist(i)) for i in range(s.n)])


H = {k: session_psths(s) for k, s in S.items()}
LR = {}
rng = np.random.default_rng(101)
t0 = time.time()
for k, s in S.items():
    LR[k] = [pfc2.lr_test(H[k][i], s.left, rng) for i in range(s.n)]
print("left-right permutation tests:", sum(len(v) for v in LR.values()), "cells in", round(time.time() - t0), "s")
G = pfc2.GRID


def selective(res, lo, hi, reading):
    """(a) any part of a significant segment in [lo, hi]; (b) the global band broken in [lo, hi]."""
    D0, point, glob, gp = res
    inr = (G >= lo) & (G <= hi)
    if reading == "a":
        return any(inr[a:b + 1].any() for a, b in pfc2.segments(point, glob))
    return bool((glob & inr).any())


# null check: the same test with the trial labels shuffled once per cell
rng0 = np.random.default_rng(102)
null = [pfc2.lr_test(H[k][i], rng0.permutation(s.left), rng0)[3] <= 0.05 for k, s in S.items() for i in range(s.n)]
print(f"false positive rate with shuffled labels (global, anywhere): {np.mean(null):.3f} of {len(null)} cells (level 0.05)")

fig2c-synchrony-by-layer¶

About 10% of layer 2/3 neurons and 20% of layer 5 neurons fire at least one spike in a given 100 ms window, and this fraction is roughly constant across the maze.

Windows of 100 ms tile each trial from its start (end of the nose-poke) to its end (trial table); a window's position is the position file's at its centre. Reading (a) the two Figure 2a sessions: only the layer 2/3 session (EE188) is in the data set; reading (b) all sessions of each layer, the windows pooled.

In [8]:
def sync_windows(s, width=0.1):
    fr, pos = [], []
    for t0, t1 in s.NP[:, 1:3]:
        edges = np.arange(t0, t1 - width + 1e-9, width)
        for a in edges:
            i, j = np.searchsorted(s.t, [a, a + width])
            fr.append(len(np.unique(s.u[i:j])) / s.n)
            f = min(int((a + width / 2) * pfc2.WHL_RATE), len(s.whl) - 1)
            pos.append(s.whl[f, 6] - 1 if s.whl[f, 6] > 0 else np.nan)
    return np.array(fr), np.array(pos)


SYNC = {k: sync_windows(s) for k, s in S.items()}


def sync_summary(keys):
    fr = np.concatenate([SYNC[k][0] for k in keys])
    pos = np.concatenate([SYNC[k][1] for k in keys])
    ok = ~np.isnan(pos)
    tenth = [fr[ok & (pos >= a / 10) & (pos < (a + 1) / 10 + (a == 9))].mean() for a in range(10)]
    return 100 * fr.mean(), 100 * np.array(tenth), len(fr), np.mean(~ok)


for k in S:
    m, tn, nw, miss = sync_summary([k])
    print(f"{k} ({S[k].layer}, {S[k].n} cells): {m:5.1f}% over {nw} windows; per tenth {np.round(tn, 1)}")
print()

fig2-population-uniform¶

Individual neurons fire transiently at specific locations, but the population as a whole fires relatively uniformly over the whole maze.

The peak position of each cell is that of the larger of its left and right PSTH peaks (Figure 2a orders cells by peak position in each condition). Only the layer 2/3 Figure 2a session (EE188) is in the data set; the layer 5 sessions of rat FF are shown as a variant.

In [9]:
def uniformity(k):
    s = S[k]
    PL = H[k][:, s.left].mean(axis=1)
    PR = H[k][:, ~s.left].mean(axis=1)
    peak = np.where(PL.max(1) >= PR.max(1), G[PL.argmax(1)], G[PR.argmax(1)])
    counts = np.histogram(peak, bins=np.linspace(0, 1, 11))[0]
    share = counts / (s.n / 10)
    chi = stats.chisquare(counts)
    pop = H[k].mean(axis=(0, 1))
    tenth = np.array([pop[(G >= a / 10) & (G < (a + 1) / 10)].mean() for a in range(10)])
    rel = tenth / pop.mean()
    ok = (share.max() <= 2) & (share.min() >= 0.5) & np.all(np.abs(rel - 1) <= 0.5)
    print(f"{k} ({s.layer}, {s.n} cells): peaks per tenth {counts.tolist()}, share of expected "
          f"{share.min():.2f} to {share.max():.2f}; chi-square against uniform {chi.statistic:.1f}, p = {chi.pvalue:.3f}; "
          f"population mean rate per tenth / overall mean {rel.min():.2f} to {rel.max():.2f}; criterion met: {ok}")
    return peak, PL, PR


peak188, PL188, PR188 = uniformity("EE188")
for k in L5:
    uniformity(k)

for t0_, t1_ in s.NP[:, 1:3]:
    f = np.arange(int(t0_ * pfc2.WHL_RATE), min(int(t1_ * pfc2.WHL_RATE) + 1, len(w)))
    f = f[(w[f, 6] > 0) & (w[f, 0] > 0)]
    tb = np.minimum(((w[f, 6] - 1) * 10).astype(int), 9)
    occ += np.bincount(tb, minlength=10) / pfc2.WHL_RATE
    two = w[f, 2] > 0
    mx = np.where(two, (w[f, 0] + w[f, 2]) / 2, w[f, 0])
    my = np.where(two, (w[f, 1] + w[f, 3]) / 2, w[f, 1])
    v = np.hypot(np.diff(mx), np.diff(my)) * pfc2.WHL_RATE
    for a in range(10):
        spd[a] += list(v[(tb[1:] == a) & (np.diff(f) == 1)])
print("EE188 time per trial in each tenth of the maze (s): " + ", ".join(f"{x:.2f}" for x in occ / len(s.NP)))
print("EE188 median speed in each tenth (pixels/s): " + ", ".join(f"{np.median(x):.0f}" for x in spd))

Result: not reproduced. In EE188 the cells' peak positions are not spread over the maze: 17 and 61 of 117 peak in the first and last tenths and some tenths hold none (chi-square p < 0.001), and the population mean rate per tenth ranges from 0.57 to 2.33 times its mean. The layer 5 sessions of rat FF show the same (variant). The PSTHs count spikes per unit of normalised length per trial, as the Methods define them, so they are higher where the rat spends more time: in EE188 it spends 0.86 s per trial in the first tenth and 2.89 s in the last, against 0.47 to 0.71 s in the others (median speed 81 and 22 pixels/s, against 138 to 198).

lifetime-width¶

Most neurons are active over a similar stretch of the maze, 0.27 (62 cm) +/- 0.17 (39 cm) of normalised length (mean +/- s.d.), measured between the 50% boundaries of the peak rate.

Readings of the claims file: PSTH (a) all trials, (b) left and right as two entries, (c) the condition with the higher peak; width (i) the contiguous run around the peak above 50%, (ii) the total length above 50%; cells (x) the Figure 2a sessions (EE188 only here), (y) all cells.

In [10]:
def widths(P, how):
    out = []
    for p in P:
        above = p >= 0.5 * p.max()
        if how == "ii":
            out.append(above.mean())
        else:
            k = p.argmax()
            a = b = k
            while a > 0 and above[a - 1]:
                a -= 1
            while b < len(p) - 1 and above[b + 1]:
                b += 1
            out.append((b - a + 1) / len(p))
    return np.array(out)


def psth_sets(keys, which):
    P = []
    for k in keys:
        s = S[k]
        PL = H[k][:, s.left].mean(1)
        PR = H[k][:, ~s.left].mean(1)
        if which == "a":
            P.append(H[k].mean(1))
        elif which == "b":
            P += [PL, PR]
        else:
            P.append(np.where((PL.max(1) >= PR.max(1))[:, None], PL, PR))
    P = np.concatenate(P)
    return P[P.max(1) > 0]


WIDTH = {}
for cells, keys in [("x", ["EE188"]), ("y", list(S))]:
    for which in "abc":
        for how in ("i", "ii"):
            w = widths(psth_sets(keys, which), how)
            WIDTH[(which, how, cells)] = (w.mean(), w.std(ddof=1))
            ok = abs(w.mean() - 0.27) <= 0.17 and abs(w.std(ddof=1) - 0.17) <= 0.017

                  f"{w.std(ddof=1):.3f}, range {w.min():.3f} to {w.max():.3f}; both within tolerance: {ok}")

trajectory-divergence¶

Left and right running paths overlap in the stem and diverge significantly from position 0.30; head directions diverge from 0.24.

From the position file of the Figure 2a layer 2/3 session (EE188), per trial the mean of each variable in 100 bins of normalised position (empty bins filled by linear interpolation along the trial), then the permutation test of the shared method at global level 0.01 on the left minus right difference. The path is (a) the lateral coordinate of the LED midpoint or (b) its distance to the mean path of all trials. The claims file names the lateral coordinate x; in this position file the stem runs along x and the arms separate along y (the mean paths are printed and plotted below), so the lateral coordinate is y, and x is shown as a variant; head direction is the angle from LED 1 to LED 2, compared through the circular difference of the condition means. The binning, and the absence of smoothing, are standard choices; the smoothed version (kernel 0.05) is a variant. All sessions are a variant.

In [11]:
NB = 100
GB = (np.arange(NB) + 0.5) / NB


def trial_paths(s):
    w = s.whl
    out = []
    for r, (t0, t1) in enumerate(s.NP[:, 1:3]):
        f = np.arange(int(t0 * pfc2.WHL_RATE), min(int(t1 * pfc2.WHL_RATE) + 1, len(w)))
        f = f[(w[f, 6] > 0) & (w[f, 0] > 0)]
        d = w[f, 6] - 1
        b = np.minimum((d * NB).astype(int), NB - 1)
        two = w[f, 2] > 0
        # LED midpoint where both LEDs are tracked, LED 1 alone otherwise
        mx = np.where(two, (w[f, 0] + w[f, 2]) / 2, w[f, 0])
        my = np.where(two, (w[f, 1] + w[f, 3]) / 2, w[f, 1])
        hd = np.where(two, np.arctan2(w[f, 3] - w[f, 1], w[f, 2] - w[f, 0]), np.nan)
        vals = []
        for v in (mx, my, np.cos(hd), np.sin(hd)):
            okv = ~np.isnan(v)
            sm = np.bincount(b[okv], v[okv], NB)
            n = np.bincount(b[okv], minlength=NB)
            m = np.where(n > 0, sm / np.maximum(n, 1), np.nan)
            ok = ~np.isnan(m)
            m = np.interp(np.arange(NB), np.flatnonzero(ok), m[ok]) if ok.sum() > 1 else np.full(NB, np.nan)
            vals.append(m)
        out.append(vals)
    return np.array(out)  # trials x 4 x NB


def perm_stat(X, labels, rng, M, stat, alpha):
    labels = np.asarray(labels, bool)
    D = np.empty((M + 1, X.shape[-1]))
    for j in range(M + 1):
        lab = labels if j == 0 else rng.permutation(labels)
        D[j] = stat(X, lab)
    point, glob, gp = pfc2.global_test(D, alpha, "two")
    return D[0], point, glob, gp


def stat_x(X, lab):
    return X[lab, 0].mean(0) - X[~lab, 0].mean(0)


def stat_y(X, lab):
    return X[lab, 1].mean(0) - X[~lab, 1].mean(0)


def stat_dist(X, lab):
    mx, my = X[:, 0].mean(0), X[:, 1].mean(0)
    dist = np.hypot(X[:, 0] - mx, X[:, 1] - my)
    return dist[lab].mean(0) - dist[~lab].mean(0)


def stat_hd(X, lab):
    aL = np.arctan2(X[lab, 3].mean(0), X[lab, 2].mean(0))
    aR = np.arctan2(X[~lab, 3].mean(0), X[~lab, 2].mean(0))
    return np.angle(np.exp(1j * (aL - aR)))


def first_sig(res):
    D0, point, glob, gp = res
    if not glob.any():
        return np.nan, np.nan
    g = np.flatnonzero(glob)[0]
    a = g
    while a > 0 and point[a - 1]:
        a -= 1
    return GB[g], GB[a]


def smooth100(X):
    from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter1d
    return gaussian_filter1d(X, 0.05 * NB, axis=-1, mode="nearest")


rng = np.random.default_rng(103)
TRAJ = {}
for k in ["EE188"] + [k for k in S if k != "EE188"]:
    s = S[k]
    X = trial_paths(s)
    good = ~np.isnan(X[:, :2]).any(axis=(1, 2))
    X, lab = X[good], s.left[good]
    hd_ok = not np.isnan(X[:, 2:]).any()
    row = []
    for name, stat in [("path a (lateral, y)", stat_y), ("path b (distance to mean path)", stat_dist),
                       ("path, x (along the stem)", stat_x), ("head direction", stat_hd)]:
        if name == "head direction" and not hd_ok:
            row.append("head direction: LED 2 not tracked")
            continue
        for sm in (False, True):
            r = perm_stat(smooth100(X) if sm else X, lab, rng, 1000, stat, 0.01)
            g, a = first_sig(r)
            TRAJ[(k, name, sm)] = (g, a)
            row.append(f"{name}{' smoothed' if sm else ''}: first global {g:.2f} (segment from {a:.2f})")
    print(f"{k} ({good.sum()} of {len(good)} trials with positions): " + "; ".join(row))
    if k == "EE188":
        print()
for name in ("path a (lateral, y)", "path b (distance to mean path)", "path, x (along the stem)"):
    g = TRAJ[("EE188", name, False)][0]
    h = TRAJ[("EE188", "head direction", False)][0]

Result: partially reproduced. In EE188 the lateral coordinate (y; the stem runs along x in this position file, as the mean paths show) first differs significantly between left and right trials at 0.28 (reading a), within 0.30 +- 0.03; the distance to the mean path (reading b) differs from 0.43 and the x coordinate from 0.48. Head direction differs from 0.01 under every reading, against 0.24, although left and right trials start 2 pixels apart. The difference lies in the first few hundredths of the maze: at 0.005 to 0.025 the mean head direction of left trials is 98 to 112 degrees and that of right trials 67 degrees (difference 31 to 45 degrees, s.d. over trials 28 to 40), at 0.055 the difference is 11 degrees and from 0.105 on 0 to 8 degrees. So the rat leaves the nose-poke with its head turned differently on left and right trials and then runs down the stem with the same heading; how the paper's head direction at 0.24 treats this start is not said. Other sessions give 0.01 to 0.43 for the lateral coordinate; head direction can be computed only in EE152 (0.17) and EE165 (0.26).

side-arm-selectivity-by-layer¶

In the side arms (positions 0.5 to 1) the fraction of neurons firing differently on left and right trials is almost twice as large in layer 5 (40%) as in layer 2/3 (22%).

All cells of each layer, pooled over rats and sessions (Figure 2b legend). Readings: a cell counts when (a) any part of a significant segment lies in 0.5 to 1, or (b) the global band is broken within 0.5 to 1. The null rate of the test is printed above (labels shuffled).

def layer_fraction(keys, lo, hi, reading):
    v = [selective(LR[k][i], lo, hi, reading) for k in keys for i in range(S[k].n)]
    return 100 * np.mean(v), int(np.sum(v)), len(v)

odor-selective-fraction¶

About a quarter of neurons (26% in one layer 2/3 session) fire at significantly different rates during nose-poking for the two odors.

Rate during each trial's nose-poke, left (one odor) against right (the other) trials, t-test at p < 0.05, session EE188 (the Figure 2a layer 2/3 session); readings (a) Student, (b) Welch. The paper's window is the "duration of nose-poking, detected by a photoelectric sensor" (Supplementary Figure 6A legend). The trial table gives only the first poke's onset and the last poke's end, so its window includes the pauses between pokes; the sensor channels of the session's .eeg file (97 and 98) give each poke, and the rate over the sensor-detected pokes alone is the main result. The table's window, and the other sessions (which have only the table), are variants.

In [14]:
def nosepoke_rates(s):
    R = np.zeros((s.ntrials, s.n))
    for r, (a, b) in enumerate(s.NP[:, :2]):
        i, j = np.searchsorted(s.t, [a, b])
        R[r] = np.bincount(s.u[i:j], minlength=s.n) / (b - a)
    return R


ODOR = {}
for k, s in S.items():
    R = nosepoke_rates(s)
    for reading, eq in (("a", True), ("b", False)):
        with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
            p = stats.ttest_ind(R[s.left], R[~s.left], equal_var=eq).pvalue
        ODOR[(k, reading)] = (p < 0.05, R[s.left].mean(0) - R[~s.left].mean(0), p)
    if k == "EE188":
        for reading in "ab":
            sig = ODOR[(k, reading)][0]
            print(f"EE188 reading {reading}: {100 * sig.mean():.1f}% ({sig.sum()}/{s.n}) odor selective; "
                  f"within 26 +- 2.6: {abs(100 * sig.mean() - 26) <= 2.6}")
        print(f"nose-poke durations EE188: median {np.median(s.NP[:, 1] - s.NP[:, 0]):.1f} s, range "
              f"{np.min(s.NP[:, 1] - s.NP[:, 0]):.1f} to {np.max(s.NP[:, 1] - s.NP[:, 0]):.1f} s")
print("other sessions, reading a:", {k: f"{100 * ODOR[(k, 'a')][0].mean():.0f}%" for k in S if k != "EE188"})
allsig = np.concatenate([ODOR[(k, "a")][0] for k in S])
print(f"all sessions, reading a: {100 * allsig.mean():.1f}% of {len(allsig)} cells")

# The sensor-detected nose-poke (Supplementary Figure 6A legend: "duration of nose-poking, detected
# by a photoelectric sensor"). The trial table gives only the first poke's onset and the last
# poke's end, so the window above includes the pauses between pokes. The session's .eeg file
# holds the two sensor channels (97, right trials; 98, left trials; data description, page 1),
# which give every poke. Rate: spikes during the pokes of the trial's channel within the trial
# table's window, over their summed duration.
sens = raw["EE188 nose-poke sensors"]
PK = {1: pfc2.poke_intervals(sens[:, 0]), 2: pfc2.poke_intervals(sens[:, 1])}
s = S["EE188"]
RS = np.zeros((s.ntrials, s.n))
npk, nother, mis, dur = [], [], [], []
for r, (a, b, _, side) in enumerate(s.NP):
    iv = PK[int(side)][(PK[int(side)][:, 1] > a - 0.01) & (PK[int(side)][:, 0] < b + 0.01)]
    other = PK[3 - int(side)]
    nother.append(int(((other[:, 1] > a) & (other[:, 0] < b)).sum()))
    npk.append(len(iv))
    mis.append(max(abs(iv[0, 0] - a), abs(iv[-1, 1] - b)))
    dur.append((iv[:, 1] - iv[:, 0]).sum())
    for x0, x1 in iv:
        i, j = np.searchsorted(s.t, [x0, x1])
        RS[r] += np.bincount(s.u[i:j], minlength=s.n)
    RS[r] /= dur[-1]
dur = np.array(dur)
print(f"EE188 sensors: pokes detected, right channel {len(PK[1])}, left channel {len(PK[2])}; per trial {min(npk)} to "
      f"{max(npk)} pokes on the trial's channel, {sum(nother)} on the other channel within the trial windows; first onset "
      f"and last end match the trial table to within {1000 * max(mis):.1f} ms")
print(f"summed poke duration per trial: median {np.median(dur):.2f} s, range {dur.min():.2f} to {dur.max():.2f} s "
      f"(left {np.median(dur[s.left]):.2f} s, right {np.median(dur[~s.left]):.2f} s); first onset to last end median "
      f"{np.median(s.NP[:, 1] - s.NP[:, 0]):.2f} s")
for reading, eq in (("a", True), ("b", False)):
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
        p = stats.ttest_ind(RS[s.left], RS[~s.left], equal_var=eq).pvalue
    sig = p < 0.05
    ODOR[("EE188", reading + "-sensor")] = (sig, RS[s.left].mean(0) - RS[~s.left].mean(0), p)
    print(f"EE188 reading {reading}, sensor-detected pokes: {100 * sig.mean():.1f}% ({sig.sum()}/{s.n}) odor selective; "
          f"within 26 +- 2.6: {abs(100 * sig.mean() - 26) <= 2.6}")

Result: not reproduced. In EE188, with the rate over the sensor-detected pokes (the paper's window), 30.8% of cells (36/117, Student's t-test; Welch 29.1%) differ between left and right trials, against 26 +- 2.6. With the trial table's window from the first poke to the end of the last, which includes the pauses between pokes, 45.3% (Welch 42.7%), and 32.4% over all sessions. The summed poke duration is shorter on left trials (median 1.52 s) than on right (3.05 s).

odor-unrelated-to-stem¶

Neurons' odor preference during nose-poking is unrelated to their left-right differences in the stem and side arms.

Session EE188. Readings (a) Fisher exact test of odor-selective (reading a of the odor claim, from the sensor-detected pokes) against selective in the region (reading a of the arm claims); (b) Spearman correlation across cells of the nose-poke rate difference (left minus right) and the mean left minus right PSTH in the region. The claims file asks for a correlation at p < 0.05 without naming the coefficient; Spearman is used, as the rate differences are heavy tailed and a rank correlation is not driven by a few high-rate cells, and Pearson is shown. The odor preference from the trial table's window is a variant.

In [15]:
s = S["EE188"]
for window, key in (("sensor-detected pokes", "a-sensor"), ("first poke to end of last (variant)", "a")):
    od_sig, od_diff, _ = ODOR[("EE188", key)]
    assoc = False
    print(f"odor preference from the {window}:")
    for name, lo, hi in (("stem 0-0.3", 0.0, 0.3), ("side arms 0.5-1", 0.5, 1.0)):
        reg = np.array([selective(LR["EE188"][i], lo, hi, "a") for i in range(s.n)])
        tab = np.array([[np.sum(od_sig & reg), np.sum(od_sig & ~reg)], [np.sum(~od_sig & reg), np.sum(~od_sig & ~reg)]])
        odds, pf = stats.fisher_exact(tab)
        inr = (G >= lo) & (G <= hi)
        dreg = np.array([LR["EE188"][i][0][inr].mean() for i in range(s.n)])
        rs = stats.spearmanr(od_diff, dreg)
        rp = stats.pearsonr(od_diff, dreg)
        same_sign = (odds > 1 and pf < 0.05) or (rs.statistic > 0 and rs.pvalue < 0.05)
        assoc |= same_sign
        print(f"  {name}: table [[odor & region, odor only], [region only, neither]] = {tab.tolist()}, Fisher odds "
              f"{odds:.2f}, p = {pf:.3f}; Spearman r = {rs.statistic:.3f}, p = {rs.pvalue:.3f}; Pearson r = "
              f"{rp.statistic:.3f}, p = {rp.pvalue:.2g}")
    print("  an association with the same sign of preference at p < 0.05 in either region:", assoc)

  side arms 0.5-1: table [[odor & region, odor only], [region only, neither]] = [[22, 14], [37, 44]], Fisher odds 1.87, p = 0.161; Spearman r = 0.237, p = 0.010; Pearson r = -0.007, p = 0.94

  side arms 0.5-1: table [[odor & region, odor only], [region only, neither]] = [[30, 23], [29, 35]], Fisher odds 1.57, p = 0.267; Spearman r = 0.134, p = 0.150; Pearson r = -0.176, p = 0.057

Result: not reproduced, resting on an assumption. With the odor preference from the sensor-detected pokes, the Spearman correlation of the nose-poke difference with the side-arm difference is 0.237 (p = 0.010), an association with the same sign of preference; the Fisher tests give p = 0.549 (stem) and 0.161 (side arms), and the stem correlation is of opposite sign (Spearman -0.155, p = 0.095; Pearson -0.278, p = 0.0024). The outcome rests on the coefficient: with Pearson the side-arm correlation is -0.007 (p = 0.94) and no association has the same sign. With the trial table's window (variant) no same-sign association is found, and the stem shows an opposite-sign one (Spearman -0.184, p = 0.047; Pearson -0.411). The criterion counts only same-sign associations; whether the paper's "no reliable relationship" excludes the opposite-sign ones is put to a reader.

retrospective-coding-rare¶

Only a small fraction of neurons fire differently according to the reward location of the previous trial.

Trials are labelled by the side of the trial before them in the trial table; the first trial of each session has no label and is left out. The table lists correct trials only, so where an error trial was left out, the trial before is the previous correct trial (a deviation). The current-trial fraction is computed on the same trials. Readings (a) the Figure 2a session (EE188, layer 2/3; the layer 5 session is not in the data set), (b) all sessions of each layer.

In [16]:

                for i in range(s.n)]
    same = np.mean(prev == cur)
    if k == "EE188":

speed-not-correlated¶

Firing rates show no net positive relationship with running speed; the distribution of rate-speed correlations is symmetric around zero.

Supplementary Figure 3C: within trials (trial start to end), 0.5 s bins; the speed of each bin is the LED midpoint's (LED 1 where LED 2 is not tracked) path length over the bin; the rate is the spike count over 0.5 s; one Pearson correlation per cell over all bins of its session. Two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test of the correlations against 0, over all cells and within the putative pyramidal cells and interneurons, typed by the files' CellsInfo; the types from the connections (G-b B-a W-a C-a) are defined further down and their correlations are printed in the cell-type-fractions section, as a variant.

In [17]:
def speed_corr(s):
    rows, cnt = [], []
    w = s.whl
    for t0, t1 in s.NP[:, 1:3]:
        for a in np.arange(t0, t1 - 0.5 + 1e-9, 0.5):
            f = np.arange(int(a * pfc2.WHL_RATE), int((a + 0.5) * pfc2.WHL_RATE) + 1)
            f = f[f < len(w)]
            ok = w[f, 0] > 0
            if ok.sum() < 3:
                continue
            two = w[f, 2] > 0
            x = np.where(two, (w[f, 0] + w[f, 2]) / 2, w[f, 0])[ok]
            y = np.where(two, (w[f, 1] + w[f, 3]) / 2, w[f, 1])[ok]
            rows.append(np.sum(np.hypot(np.diff(x), np.diff(y))) / (len(x) - 1) * pfc2.WHL_RATE)
            i, j = np.searchsorted(s.t, [a, a + 0.5])
            cnt.append(np.bincount(s.u[i:j], minlength=s.n))
    sp = np.array(rows)
    C = np.array(cnt, float)
    r = np.array([np.corrcoef(sp, C[:, i])[0, 1] if C[:, i].std() > 0 else np.nan for i in range(s.n)])
    return r, len(sp)


SPEED = {}
for k, s in S.items():
    SPEED[k], nb = speed_corr(s)

w_all = stats.wilcoxon(r_all)

      f"fraction positive {np.mean(r_all > 0):.2f}, Wilcoxon p = {w_all.pvalue:.2g}; "
      f"median significantly above 0: {np.median(r_all) > 0 and w_all.pvalue < 0.05}")
print(f"range of r: {r_all.min():.2f} to {r_all.max():.2f}")
for k in S:
    r = SPEED[k][~np.isnan(SPEED[k])]
    print(f"  {k}: median r = {np.median(r):.3f}, n = {len(r)}")
for r_ in ("EE", "FF", "GG"):
    r = np.concatenate([SPEED[k] for k in S if S[k].rat == r_])
    r = r[~np.isnan(r)]
    print(f"  rat {r_}: median r = {np.median(r):.3f}, n = {len(r)}, Wilcoxon p = {stats.wilcoxon(r).pvalue:.2g}")
ty = np.concatenate([S[k].celltype_file for k in S])
rr = np.concatenate([SPEED[k] for k in S])
for t, name in ((1, "pyramidal"), (2, "interneuron")):
    v = rr[(ty == t) & ~np.isnan(rr)]
    print(f"  CellsInfo {name}: median r = {np.median(v):.3f}, n = {len(v)}, Wilcoxon p = {stats.wilcoxon(v).pvalue:.2g}")

By the files' CellsInfo types the median is -0.007 for pyramidal cells (p = 0.065) and -0.078 for interneurons (p = 3.2e-05); by the connection-based types (G-b B-a W-a C-a), -0.015 (p = 0.041) and -0.088 (p = 0.065).

population-vector-width¶

Population vector correlations fall off over similar distances throughout the maze, 0.18 +/- 0.087 of normalised length in layer 2/3 and 0.27 +/- 0.13 in layer 5.

Population vectors of the cells' PSTHs at the 200 positions, Pearson correlation between positions; width at a position, the contiguous length around the diagonal over which the correlation stays above half its diagonal value (1); mean +/- s.d. over positions. Readings (a) left and right PSTHs concatenated in each vector, (b) all trials. Sessions: the Figure 2a layer 2/3 session (EE188; the layer 5 one is not in the data set), and all sessions of each layer pooled into one vector (the variant the claims file names), which gives the only layer 5 value. Whether each cell's PSTH is normalised before the correlation is not said; raw rates, rates over the cell's peak (as Figure 2a displays them) and z-scored rates are all run.

In [18]:
def pv_width(keys, which, norm):
    P = []
    for k in keys:
        s = S[k]
        if which == "a":
            P.append(np.concatenate([H[k][:, s.left].mean(1), H[k][:, ~s.left].mean(1)], axis=0))
        else:
            P.append(H[k].mean(1))
    P = np.concatenate(P)
    P = P[P.std(1) > 0]
    if norm == "peak":
        P = P / P.max(1, keepdims=True)
    elif norm == "z":
        P = (P - P.mean(1, keepdims=True)) / P.std(1, keepdims=True)
    C = np.corrcoef(P.T)
    wd = []
    for x in range(len(C)):
        above = C[x] > 0.5
        a = b = x
        while a > 0 and above[a - 1]:
            a -= 1
        while b < len(C) - 1 and above[b + 1]:
            b += 1
        wd.append((b - a + 1) / len(C))
    return np.array(wd), C

        PV[(label, which, norm)] = (wd.mean(), wd.std(ddof=1))
        print(f"{norm:4s} {label}, reading {which}: width {wd.mean():.3f} +- {wd.std(ddof=1):.3f} (range {wd.min():.3f} to "
              f"{wd.max():.3f}); correlations {C.min():.2f} to {C.max():.2f}")

Result: reproduced, resting on an assumption. With raw rates the population vector correlations stay above 0.35 everywhere and above 0.5 almost everywhere, so the width is close to the whole maze (0.96 to 1.00) and the claim fails; with each cell's PSTH divided by its peak (the assumption), EE188 gives 0.239 (reading a) and the pooled layer 5 sessions 0.300, within 0.18 +- 0.087 and 0.27 +- 0.13, and z-scored PSTHs give 0.182 and 0.204; all normalised readings match except the pooled layer 2/3 peak-normalised reading b (0.268). The s.d. over positions (0.026 to 0.086) is smaller than the paper's 0.087 and 0.13; the criterion does not test it. The layer 5 value comes from the pooled sessions, as the Figure 2a layer 5 session is not in the data set.

Monosynaptic connections¶

For every session, the cross-correlogram of every ordered pair of cells over the whole session (Figure 3b includes the intertrial intervals), against 1,000 surrogates in which every spike of every cell is jittered uniformly on [-5, +5] ms (Methods). Connection: the counts break the global 99% band anywhere in [1, 4] ms, above (excitatory, a peak) or below (inhibitory, a trough). Readings of the claims file: bin width B-a 1 ms or B-b 0.5 ms; width rule W-a the global band test alone, W-b also requiring the run of bins beyond the pointwise 99% band around the extreme to span 2 ms or less. The global band is built from the maximum and minimum of each surrogate over [-5, +5] ms (Methods, "Identifying monosynaptic interactions"), and the Methods define a band's global acceptance level as "the proportion of the original and the resampled data sets i that lie completely within the pointwise bands" ("Multiple hypothesis testing and global bands"), and the global band at level a as "the minimal pointwise band with global acceptance level a", found by "a stepping procedure". The band is therefore stepped inwards, excluding the k largest surrogate maxima and the k smallest minima, for as long as at least 99% of the surrogates lie entirely within both sides (G-b, used for every claim). Taking 1% on each side (G-a), the reading of the first version of this notebook, is shown as a variant for every claim that uses the connections. Both are checked against the connections the authors list for session EE188 (pairs_all of EE188_example.mat), and the fraction of surrogates that lie entirely within both bands is printed.

CONN = {}
JOINT = {"G-b": [], "G-a": []}
GS = ("G-b", "G-a")
t0 = time.time()
for bw, tag in ((0.001, "B-a"), (0.0005, "B-b")):
    for k, s in S.items():
        rng = np.random.default_rng(200 + list(S).index(k) + (0 if tag == "B-a" else 50))
        obs, sur = pfc2.ccg_jitter(s.t, s.u, s.n, rng, bw, nsur=1000)
        for gs, gside in (("G-b", "step"), ("G-a", 0.01)):
            c = pfc2.detect_connections(obs, sur, bw, gside=gside)
            CONN[(k, tag, gs)] = {"exc": c["exc"], "inh": c["inh"], "width": c["width"]}
            JOINT[gs].append(c["joint"][~np.eye(s.n, dtype=bool)])
        del obs, sur, c
print("jitter CCGs of", sum(s.n * (s.n - 1) for s in S.values()), "ordered pairs, two bin widths, in",
      round(time.time() - t0), "s")
for gs in GS:
    v = np.concatenate(JOINT[gs])
    print(f"{gs}: fraction of surrogates lying entirely within both global bands, over pairs and bin widths: median "
          f"{np.median(v):.4f}, 5th to 95th percentile {np.percentile(v, 5):.4f} to {np.percentile(v, 95):.4f} (target 0.99)")


def conns(k, B, W, G="G-b"):
    c = CONN[(k, B, G)]
    E, I = c["exc"].copy(), c["inh"].copy()
    if W == "W-b":
        E &= c["width"] <= 2
        I &= c["width"] <= 2
    return E, I


COMBOS = [(b, w) for b in ("B-a", "B-b") for w in ("W-a", "W-b")]

Detector check on the data. In EE188 every cell's spike train is moved in time and the detector is run again (B-a W-a, 1,000 surrogates); any connection found is a false positive. Two shifts: (1) each cell by its own random circular offset of 10 s or more, which removes every dependence between the cells; (2) the cells in a random order, shifted by 25 ms times their rank, so that every pair is offset by 25 ms or more: short-lag interactions are removed while rate changes slower than the offsets (behaviour, position on the maze) stay shared for most pairs.

In [20]:
s = S["EE188"]
rng = np.random.default_rng(250)
T = max(s.t.max(), s.duration) + 1
NULLSHIFT = {}
npairs = s.n * (s.n - 1)
for shift in ("circular", "rank x 25 ms"):
    off = rng.uniform(10, T - 10, s.n) if shift == "circular" else 0.025 * rng.permutation(s.n)
    tsh = (s.t + off[s.u]) % T
    o = np.argsort(tsh, kind="stable")
    obs, sur = pfc2.ccg_jitter(tsh[o], s.u[o], s.n, rng, 0.001, nsur=1000)
    for gs, gside in (("G-b", "step"), ("G-a", 0.01)):
        c = pfc2.detect_connections(obs, sur, 0.001, gside=gside)
        NULLSHIFT[(shift, gs)] = (c["exc"].sum() / npairs, c["inh"].sum() / npairs)
        E0, I0 = conns("EE188", "B-a", "W-a", gs)
        print(f"EE188 shifted ({shift}), {gs} B-a W-a: excitatory {c['exc'].sum()} ({100 * NULLSHIFT[(shift, gs)][0]:.2f}% "
              f"of {npairs} directed pairs), inhibitory {c['inh'].sum()} ({100 * NULLSHIFT[(shift, gs)][1]:.2f}%); "
              f"unshifted: excitatory {E0.sum()} ({100 * E0.sum() / npairs:.2f}%), inhibitory {I0.sum()} ({100 * I0.sum() / npairs:.2f}%)")
    del obs, sur, c

connection-counts¶

Of 62,408 directed cell pairs, 495 (0.79%) show a short-latency narrow peak or trough in the cross-correlogram, 0.55% excitatory and 0.24% inhibitory, and 0.17% of pairs are reciprocally connected.

Reciprocal: unordered pairs connected in both directions (any type); denominator (a) directed pairs, (b) unordered pairs. The data set holds three of the paper's four rats.

Result: not reproduced. The data set gives 40,240 directed pairs (three of four rats, against 62,408). With the Methods' global band (G-b), 0.94 to 1.32% of pairs are connected, 0.84 to 0.97% excitatory and 0.11 to 0.39% inhibitory over the four B and W combinations, against 0.79%, 0.55% and 0.24%; with 1% on each side (G-a), 1.07 to 1.50%, 0.94 to 1.09% and 0.14 to 0.47%. No combination puts the three directed values within tolerance. Reciprocal pairs are 0.045 to 0.199% of directed pairs under G-b; 0.179% of unordered pairs under G-a B-b W-a is the only reciprocal value within tolerance. With every train of EE188 shifted in time, the detector flags 0.12 to 0.15% of pairs as excitatory and 0.04 to 0.07% as inhibitory (G-b B-a W-a), against 0.70% and 0.26% in the unshifted data, so false positives of this kind account for part, not all, of the excess over the paper's rates. Under G-b the band holds a median 99.4% of the surrogates (5th percentile 99.0%).

cell-type-fractions¶

32.5% of units are putative pyramidal cells and 12.5% putative interneurons; 50.7% of the targets of excitatory cells themselves suppress other neurons; the ratio of pyramidal cells to interneurons is 2.82 +/- 0.51 (s.d.).

A cell with a significant excitatory connection as reference is a putative pyramidal cell, one with an inhibitory one a putative interneuron. A cell with both: C-a unclassified, C-b excluded from the denominators. The ratio: mean +/- s.d. over (a) sessions, (b) rats; units without an interneuron cannot give a ratio and are left out (counted below). Every combination is run under G-b and, as a variant, G-a.

In [22]:
def celltypes(k, B, W, C, G="G-b"):
    E, I = conns(k, B, W, G)
    pyr, inn = E.any(1), I.any(1)
    both = pyr & inn
    return pyr & ~both, inn & ~both, both


TYPES = {}
for gs in GS:
    for B, W in COMBOS:
        for C in ("C-a", "C-b"):
            npyr = nint = nboth = ntot = 0
            tgt_int = tgt = 0
            per_s, per_r = [], {}
            for k in S:
                pyr, inn, both = celltypes(k, B, W, C, gs)
                TYPES[(k, B, W, C, gs)] = (pyr, inn)
                E, I = conns(k, B, W, gs)
                npyr += pyr.sum()
                nint += inn.sum()
                nboth += both.sum()
                ntot += S[k].n - (both.sum() if C == "C-b" else 0)
                targets = E.any(0)
                tgt += targets.sum()
                tgt_int += (targets & I.any(1)).sum()
                if inn.sum() > 0:
                    per_s.append(pyr.sum() / inn.sum())
                r = S[k].rat
                per_r.setdefault(r, [0, 0])
                per_r[r][0] += pyr.sum()
                per_r[r][1] += inn.sum()
            rs = np.array(per_s)
            rr = np.array([a / b for a, b in per_r.values() if b > 0])
            fp, fi, ft = 100 * npyr / ntot, 100 * nint / ntot, 100 * tgt_int / tgt
            ok = (abs(fp - 32.5) <= 3.25, abs(fi - 12.5) <= 1.25, abs(ft - 50.7) <= 5.07,
                  abs(rs.mean() - 2.82) <= 0.51 if len(rs) else False, abs(rr.mean() - 2.82) <= 0.51 if len(rr) else False)
            print(f"{gs} {B} {W} {C}: pyramidal {fp:.1f}% ({npyr}/{ntot}), interneurons {fi:.1f}% ({nint}), both {nboth}; "
                  f"targets of excitation that are interneurons {ft:.1f}% ({tgt_int}/{tgt}); ratio per session "
                  f"{rs.mean() if len(rs) else np.nan:.2f} +- {rs.std(ddof=1) if len(rs) > 1 else np.nan:.2f} (n = {len(rs)} of {len(S)}), per rat "
                  f"{rr.mean() if len(rr) else np.nan:.2f} +- {rr.std(ddof=1) if len(rr) > 1 else np.nan:.2f} (n = {len(rr)}); within tolerance "
                  f"[pyr, int, targets, ratio a, ratio b]: {ok}")

pyr-pyr-connections¶

Monosynaptic excitation between putative pyramidal cells is rare, found in 0.12% of layer 2/3 and 0.27% of layer 5 pairs.

Excitatory connections whose target is also a putative pyramidal cell; denominator (a) all directed pairs of the layer, (b) directed pairs of two putative pyramidal cells.

for gs in GS:
    for B, W in COMBOS:
        for C in ("C-a", "C-b"):
            out = []
            for lay, keys in (("L2/3", L23), ("L5", L5)):
                npp = nall = npyrpairs = 0
                for k in keys:
                    E, I = conns(k, B, W, gs)
                    pyr, inn = TYPES[(k, B, W, C, gs)]
                    npp += (E & pyr[:, None] & pyr[None, :]).sum()
                    nall += S[k].n * (S[k].n - 1)
                    npyrpairs += pyr.sum() * (pyr.sum() - 1)
                out.append((lay, npp, 100 * npp / nall, 100 * npp / max(npyrpairs, 1)))
            ok_a = abs(out[0][2] - 0.12) <= 0.012 and abs(out[1][2] - 0.27) <= 0.027
            ok_b = abs(out[0][3] - 0.12) <= 0.012 and abs(out[1][3] - 0.27) <= 0.027
            print(f"{gs} {B} {W} {C}: " + "; ".join(f"{l} {n} connections, {a:.3f}% of all pairs, {b:.2f}% of pyramidal pairs" for l, n, a, b in out)
                  + f"; within tolerance (a) {ok_a}, (b) {ok_b}")

def largest_component(A):
    g = nx.Graph()
    g.add_edges_from(zip(*np.nonzero(A)))
    return max((len(c) for c in nx.connected_components(g)), default=0)

fig3f-distance¶

Most connected pairs are on the same shank and connection probability falls rapidly with the distance between the neurons, yet connections are found up to 1,200 um apart.

Connection probability by shank separation (200 um per shank), excitatory and inhibitory separately, with exact Clopper-Pearson 99% intervals, all sessions, under G-b and G-a.

In [26]:
def cp_interval(k, n, level=0.99):
    a = 1 - level
    lo = stats.beta.ppf(a / 2, k, n - k + 1) if k > 0 else 0.0
    hi = stats.beta.ppf(1 - a / 2, k + 1, n - k) if k < n else 1.0
    return lo, hi


for gs, (B, W) in [(g, c) for g in GS for c in COMBOS]:
    cnt = {}
    for k, s in S.items():
        E, I = conns(k, B, W, gs)
        sep = np.abs(s.shank[:, None] - s.shank[None, :]) * 200
        off = ~np.eye(s.n, dtype=bool)
        for d in np.unique(sep[off]):
            m = (sep == d) & off
            c = cnt.setdefault(d, [0, 0, 0])
            c[0] += m.sum()
            c[1] += (E & m).sum()
            c[2] += (I & m).sum()
    ds = sorted(cnt)
    same = cnt[0][1] + cnt[0][2]
    other = sum(cnt[d][1] + cnt[d][2] for d in ds if d > 0)
    p0 = (cnt[0][1] + cnt[0][2]) / cnt[0][0]
    lo0, hi0 = cp_interval(cnt[0][1] + cnt[0][2], cnt[0][0])
    lo2, hi2 = cp_interval(cnt[200][1] + cnt[200][2], cnt[200][0])
    p2 = (cnt[200][1] + cnt[200][2]) / cnt[200][0]
    far = max(d for d in ds if cnt[d][1] + cnt[d][2] > 0)
    print(f"{gs} {B} {W}: connected pairs on the same shank {same}, on other shanks {other}; same-shank probability "
          f"{100 * p0:.2f}% [{100 * lo0:.2f}, {100 * hi0:.2f}] against 200 um {100 * p2:.2f}% [{100 * lo2:.2f}, {100 * hi2:.2f}]; "
          f"largest separation with a connection {far} um; criterion met: {same > other and lo0 > hi2 and far == 1200}")
    if (B, W) == ("B-a", "W-a"):
        print(f"    {gs} B-a W-a by separation:")
        for d in ds:
            e_lo, e_hi = cp_interval(cnt[d][1], cnt[d][0])
            i_lo, i_hi = cp_interval(cnt[d][2], cnt[d][0])
            print(f"    {d:5d} um: {cnt[d][0]:6d} pairs, excitatory {100 * cnt[d][1] / cnt[d][0]:.2f}% [{100 * e_lo:.2f}, "
                  f"{100 * e_hi:.2f}], inhibitory {100 * cnt[d][2] / cnt[d][0]:.2f}% [{100 * i_lo:.2f}, {100 * i_hi:.2f}]")

Result: partially reproduced. Most connected pairs are on the same shank (352 against 195 on other shanks, G-b B-a W-a), and the same-shank probability (6.20%, 99% interval 5.41 to 7.07) is far above that at 200 um (1.24%, 0.97 to 1.56), falling with distance; but connections are found up to 1,400 um, the largest separation on the probe, not 1,200. The 1,400 um value rests on 2 excitatory and 2 inhibitory connections of 504 pairs (0.40% each, 99% interval 0.02 to 1.83%). Every B, W and G combination gives the same pattern and the same largest separation.

nearby-pyr-int-probability¶

Connection probability between nearby (under 200 um) putative pyramidal cells and interneurons is 1 to 2%.

Same-shank pairs of a putative pyramidal cell and a putative interneuron, all sessions. Readings (a) pyramidal to interneuron excitatory connections over such directed pairs, (b) a connection in either direction over unordered pairs.

for gs in GS:

            for k, s in S.items():
                E, I = conns(k, B, W, gs)
                pyr, inn = TYPES[(k, B, W, C, gs)]
                m = (s.shank[:, None] == s.shank[None, :]) & pyr[:, None] & inn[None, :]
                na += m.sum()
                ka += (E & m).sum()
                kb += ((E | I | E.T | I.T) & m).sum()
            pa_, pb_ = 100 * ka / max(na, 1), 100 * kb / max(na, 1)
            print(f"{gs} {B} {W} {C}: {na} same-shank pyramidal-interneuron pairs; (a) {ka} = {pa_:.1f}%, (b) {kb} = {pb_:.1f}%; "
                  f"in 0.9 to 2.2%: (a) {0.9 <= pa_ <= 2.2}, (b) {0.9 <= pb_ <= 2.2}")

connected-cells-trajectory-specific¶

Most putative pyramidal cells (72.2% in layer 2/3, 84.7% in layer 5) and many interneurons (58.3% and 83%) fire differently on left and right trajectories.

A cell is trajectory specific when the left-right permutation test (above) finds a significant segment anywhere. Readings (a) the identified cells of the Figure 3 sessions (EE188 for layer 2/3; the layer 5 session is not in the data set), (b) all sessions of each layer.

In [28]:
def traj_frac(keys, B, W, C, gs):
    out = {}
    for name, j in (("pyr", 0), ("int", 1)):
        v = np.concatenate([[LR[k][i][3] <= 0.05 for i in np.flatnonzero(TYPES[(k, B, W, C, gs)][j])] for k in keys])
        out[name] = (100 * v.mean() if len(v) else np.nan, int(v.sum()), len(v))
    return out


for gs, (B, W) in [(g, c) for g in GS for c in COMBOS]:
    for C in ("C-a",):

        b23 = traj_frac(L23, B, W, C, gs)
        b5 = traj_frac(L5, B, W, C, gs)
        ok_b = (abs(b23["pyr"][0] - 72.2) <= 7.22 and abs(b5["pyr"][0] - 84.7) <= 8.47 and
                abs(b23["int"][0] - 58.3) <= 5.83 and abs(b5["int"][0] - 83) <= 8.3)

no-spatial-clustering¶

Left- and right-specific neurons are not clustered on the probe but spread over the whole recorded volume.

Class per cell from its significant segments: left (left rate higher), right, both, or none. Chi-square test of shank against class in the Figure 3 session (EE188), and each session as a variant; Cramer's V.

In [29]:
def lr_class(res):
    D0, point, glob, gp = res
    segs = pfc2.segments(point, glob)
    left = any(D0[a:b + 1].mean() > 0 for a, b in segs)
    right = any(D0[a:b + 1].mean() < 0 for a, b in segs)
    return "both" if left and right else "left" if left else "right" if right else "none"


def cluster_test(k):
    s = S[k]
    cls = np.array([lr_class(r) for r in LR[k]])
    labs = ["left", "right", "both", "none"]
    sh = np.unique(s.shank)
    tab = np.array([[np.sum((s.shank == h) & (cls == c)) for c in labs] for h in sh])
    tab = tab[:, tab.sum(0) > 0]
    tab = tab[tab.sum(1) > 0]
    chi2, p, dof, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(tab)
    v = np.sqrt(chi2 / (tab.sum() * (min(tab.shape) - 1)))
    return chi2, p, v, tab, cls


chi2, p, v, tab, cls = cluster_test("EE188")
print(f"EE188: classes {dict(zip(*np.unique(cls, return_counts=True)))}; shanks x classes table {tab.tolist()}; "
      f"chi-square {chi2:.1f}, p = {p:.3f}, Cramer's V = {v:.2f}; association at p < 0.05: {p < 0.05}")
for k in S:
    if k != "EE188":
        chi2, p, v, tab, cls = cluster_test(k)
        print(f"  {k}: chi-square {chi2:.1f}, p = {p:.3f}, V = {v:.2f}, {S[k].n} cells")

Position dependence of spike transmission¶

For each excitatory connection, coincident events (1 <= tdiff <= 4 ms) are placed at the presynaptic spike's position within trials, smoothed with the 0.05 kernel and divided by the number of trials, and compared with 1,000 surrogates jittering every spike of both cells on [-5, +5] ms, one-sided for excess, global level 0.01 (Methods). Readings of the claims file: trials (a) left and right separately, a pair counting when either shows dependence, (b) all trials together; dependence (i) a globally significant region anywhere, (ii) a globally significant region and a part of the maze where the pointwise band is not broken. The connections are those of G-b B-a W-a; B-b W-a and G-a are variants. Jittering the presynaptic cell only (Supplementary Figure 12B) is run as a variant on the G-b B-a W-a connections.

In [30]:
POSDEP = {}
t0 = time.time()
rng = np.random.default_rng(300)
pairs_needed = set()
# the G-b connections are a subset of the G-a ones, so the tests are run on G-a and selected below
for B in ("B-a", "B-b"):
    for k in S:
        assert not (conns(k, B, "W-a")[0] & ~conns(k, B, "W-a", "G-a")[0]).any()
        E, _ = conns(k, B, "W-a", "G-a")
        pairs_needed |= {(k, i, j) for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(E))}
for k, i, j in sorted(pairs_needed):
    s = S[k]
    res = {}
    for name, m in (("L", s.left), ("R", ~s.left), ("all", np.ones(s.ntrials, bool))):
        S0, mu, point, glob, gp = pfc2.coincidence_test(s, i, j, rng, trials_mask=m)
        res[name] = (gp <= 0.01, bool(glob.any() and (~point).any()), point, glob, S0, mu)
    POSDEP[(k, i, j)] = res
print(f"coincidence tests on {len(POSDEP)} excitatory connections x 3 trial sets in {round(time.time() - t0)} s")


def posdep(key, trials, dep):
    r = POSDEP[key]
    sets = ("L", "R") if trials == "a" else ("all",)
    return any(r[t][0] if dep == "i" else r[t][1] for t in sets)

coincidence tests on 573 excitatory connections x 3 trial sets in 157 s

position-dependent-transmission¶

Of 343 pairs with significant excitatory monosynaptic connections, 67 show identifiable position dependence of excess short-latency coincidences.

In [31]:
for gs in GS:
    for B in ("B-a", "B-b"):
        keys = [(k, i, j) for k in S for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(conns(k, B, "W-a", gs)[0]))]
        for trials in "ab":
            for dep in ("i", "ii"):
                n = sum(posdep(x, trials, dep) for x in keys)
                ok = (abs(len(keys) - 343) <= 34.3 and abs(n - 67) <= 6.7) or abs(100 * n / len(keys) - 19.5) <= 2.0
                print(f"{gs} {B} W-a, trials {trials}, dependence {dep:2s}: {n} of {len(keys)} excitatory connections "
                      f"({100 * n / len(keys):.1f}%); counts or fraction within tolerance: {ok}")
keys = [(k, i, j) for k in S for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(conns(k, "B-a", "W-a")[0]))]
for r in ("EE", "FF", "GG"):
    kk = [x for x in keys if S[x[0]].rat == r]
    print(f"  rat {r}: {sum(posdep(x, 'a', 'i') for x in kk)} of {len(kk)} (G-b B-a, a, i)")
# variant: jittering the presynaptic cell only (Supplementary Figure 12B), G-b B-a W-a
rng1 = np.random.default_rng(302)
PRE = {}
for k, i, j in keys:
    s = S[k]
    PRE[(k, i, j)] = {name: pfc2.coincidence_test(s, i, j, rng1, trials_mask=m, jitter_post=False)[4] <= 0.01
                      for name, m in (("L", s.left), ("R", ~s.left), ("all", np.ones(s.ntrials, bool)))}
for trials in "ab":
    n = sum(any(PRE[x][t] for t in (("L", "R") if trials == "a" else ("all",))) for x in keys)
    print(f"presynaptic jitter only, G-b B-a W-a, trials {trials}, dependence i: {n} of {len(keys)} ({100 * n / len(keys):.1f}%)")
# null check: the same test with pre spikes shifted by 20 ms, which removes the monosynaptic lag
rng0 = np.random.default_rng(301)
sub = keys[::10]
fp = 0
for k, i, j in sub:
    s = S[k]
    ps = pfc2.pair_spikes(s, i, j)
    ps["tpre"] = ps["tpre"] + 0.02
    fp += pfc2.coincidence_test(s, i, j, rng0, ps=ps)[4] <= 0.01
print(f"null check, presynaptic spikes shifted by 20 ms: {fp} of {len(sub)} pairs significant (level 0.01)")

Of 389 excitatory connections (G-b B-a), 31 show position dependence (8.0%, readings a and i), 31 to 34 under the other readings, against 67 of 343 (19.5%); B-b gives 30 to 36 of 349, and G-a 31 to 36 of 387 to 439. Shifting the presynaptic spikes by 20 ms makes 0 of 39 pairs significant.

fig4-pair-156-136¶

Pair 156-136, on different shanks, keeps steady firing rates between positions 0.2 and 0.5 on left trials, yet excess short-latency coincidences occur only between 0.4 and 0.6.

Cell numbers are the data set's (CellsInfo of EE188_example.mat, the numbering of the paper's figures by the data description).

In [33]:
def example_pair(a, b, trials, seed):
    s = S["EE188"]
    i, j = idx[a], idx[b]
    m = s.left if trials == "L" else ~s.left
    S0, mu, point, glob, gp = pfc2.coincidence_test(s, i, j, np.random.default_rng(seed), trials_mask=m)
    segs = [(round(G[x] - 0.5 / pfc2.NGRID, 3), round(G[y] + 0.5 / pfc2.NGRID, 3)) for x, y in pfc2.segments(point, glob)]
    gl = np.flatnonzero(glob)
    gext = (round(G[gl[0]], 3), round(G[gl[-1]], 3)) if len(gl) else None
    return segs, gext, gp, S0, mu

Result: partially reproduced. On left trials the excess coincidences of 156-136 form a single significant region in mid-maze, from 0.325 to 0.645 by the pointwise band (global band broken from 0.372 to 0.622). Its end is within 0.6 +- 0.06, but its start is 0.075 before 0.4 (tolerance 0.04), and between 0.2 and 0.5 the rate of cell 136 varies by 59% of its maximum (cell 156 by 49%), so 136 is not steady by the criterion's 50%. The pair is a connection under the test (G-b B-a W-a) and in pairs_all.

thinning-preserves-dependence¶

In several pairs, position-dependent transmission remains after spikes are thinned so that both cells fire at a flat rate over the region examined.

Methods, "Controlling for power": in the region, spikes are removed one at a time at random within [-s, +s] of the PSTH maximum until the PSTH minimum is within 10% of the maximum, for both cells, then the position test. Pairs: the position-dependent connections (G-b B-a W-a, trials a, dependence i), on the trials where they are dependent. Regions: (a) 0.2 to 0.5 (Supplementary Figure 13A), (b) the smallest span holding the pair's significant region plus an equal length of non-significant maze next to it. Ten repetitions with fixed seeds; a pair holds when, in the majority of repetitions, a globally significant region and a non-significant part of the region remain. The thinning stops early when no spike is left within [-s, +s] of the maximum, so the ratio of each thinned PSTH's minimum to its maximum in the region is printed, and a repetition counts only when both cells reached the target (ratio 0.9 or more); the count without that condition is shown as well.

In [35]:
def thin_pair(key, tr, lo, hi, rng):
    k, i, j = key
    s = S[k]
    m = s.left if tr == "L" else ~s.left
    ps = pfc2.pair_spikes(s, i, j, m)
    kp, fp_ = pfc2.thin(ps["tpre"], ps["xpre"], ps["inpre"], lo, hi, rng)
    kq, fq_ = pfc2.thin(ps["tpost"], ps["xpost"], ps["inpost"], lo, hi, rng)
    a = kp | ~ps["inpre"]
    b = kq | ~ps["inpost"]
    p2 = {"tpre": ps["tpre"][a], "xpre": ps["xpre"][a], "inpre": kp[a], "tpost": ps["tpost"][b], "N": ps["N"]}
    S0, mu, point, glob, gp = pfc2.coincidence_test(s, i, j, rng, ps=p2)
    reg = (G >= lo) & (G <= hi)
    return bool((glob & reg).any() and (~point & reg).any()), min(fp_, fq_)

The thinning reaches its target (each cell's PSTH minimum within 10% of its maximum in the region) in 26% of thinnings in the region 0.2 to 0.5 (reading a) and 23% in reading b; it stops early when no spike is left within s of the maximum. Counting a repetition only when both cells were flattened, no pair keeps a significant and a non-significant part in the majority of 10 thinnings under reading a (16 pairs), and 1 of 36 does under reading b (EE196 8-7, 10 of 10), against at least two. Without the flatness condition 2 pairs hold under reading a, but their thinned PSTHs keep a minimum of 0 to 8% of the maximum, so their rates were not flat.

Spike order and convergence¶

fig6-depression-facilitation¶

Comparing first spikes of trains with later spikes, about equal shares of pairs show depressing (12.7%) and facilitating (10.7%) spike transmission; 32.2% of the significant pairs are on different shanks.

Presynaptic spikes are first (at least 200 ms without a spike before) or later (within 40 ms of the previous spike). For each group, the standardised peak height against jitter surrogates (100, jittering both cells on [-5, +5] ms); the difference, first minus later, is tested by shuffling the labels between the groups (500 permutations), two-sided at P < 0.10. The standardised heights grow with the square root of the number of spikes, so when the two groups differ in size the permutation distribution of the difference is not centred on 0. The two-sided P is therefore taken from the two tails of that distribution (the Methods' P+- = min(1, 2P+, 2P-)), and a pair depresses when its difference lies in the upper tail (first spikes more effective than under shuffled labels) and facilitates when it lies in the lower tail. The first version of this notebook compared absolute values with a null assumed centred on 0. A check on synthetic trains below shows that the test now finds a known effect in either direction and holds its level when first and later spikes are equally effective. The numbers of surrogates and permutations are standard choices made smaller than 1,000 for time. Readings: pairs (a) the excitatory connections, (b) all connections; height (i) largest 1 ms bin in [1, 4] ms, (ii) sum over [1, 4] ms; later spikes (x) in a train begun by a first spike, (y) any spike within 40 ms. Connections of G-b B-a W-a, with G-a as a variant.

In [36]:
# Synthetic check of the test: a presynaptic cell firing trains of 1 to 3 spikes 10 ms apart after
# silences of 0.3 to 1.5 s, a target firing at 5 Hz plus a spike 2 ms after a presynaptic spike with
# probability q_first (first spikes) or q_later (later spikes), 1,800 s.
def synth(q_first, q_later, rng):
    starts = np.cumsum(rng.uniform(0.3, 1.5, 1500))
    pre, lab = [], []
    for t in starts:
        n = rng.integers(1, 4)
        pre += [t + 0.01 * m for m in range(n)]
        lab += [m == 0 for m in range(n)]
    pre, lab = np.array(pre), np.array(lab)
    q = np.where(lab, q_first, q_later)
    post = np.sort(np.concatenate([rng.uniform(0, starts[-1] + 1, int(5 * (starts[-1] + 1))),
                                   pre[rng.random(len(pre)) < q] + 0.002]))
    return pre, post


rng = np.random.default_rng(602)
for qf, ql, name in ((0.1, 0.1, "equal efficacy"), (0.05, 0.2, "later spikes 4 times as effective"),
                     (0.2, 0.05, "first spikes 4 times as effective")):
    out = []
    for rep_ in range(20):
        pre, post = synth(qf, ql, rng)
        f, l = pfc2.train_labels(pre)
        r = pfc2.order_effect(pre, post, f, l, rng, "i", nsur=100, nperm=500)
        out.append((r[2], r[7], r[3] < 0.10, r[6]))
    d, m, sg, sd = (np.array(x) for x in zip(*out))
    print(f"synthetic, {name}, 20 runs: difference first - later mean {d.mean():.1f}, mean permuted difference {m.mean():.1f}; "
          f"significant at P < 0.10 as depression {np.sum(sg & (sd > 0))}, as facilitation {np.sum(sg & (sd < 0))}")

t0 = time.time()
rng = np.random.default_rng(600)
F6 = {}
for k, s in S.items():
    E, I = conns(k, "B-a", "W-a", "G-a")  # the G-b connections are a subset
    for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(E | I)):
        tpre, tpost = s.spikes_of(i), s.spikes_of(j)
        for ch in ("x", "y"):
            f, l = pfc2.train_labels(tpre, chained=(ch == "x"))
            if f.sum() < 5 or l.sum() < 5:
                continue
            for how in ("i", "ii"):
                F6[(k, i, j, ch, how)] = pfc2.order_effect(tpre, tpost, f, l, rng, how, nsur=100, nperm=500) + (bool(E[i, j]),)
print(f"order effects for {len(F6)} pair-reading combinations in {round(time.time() - t0)} s")
for gs in GS:
    for pairs in "ab":
        for ch in ("x", "y"):
            for how in ("i", "ii"):
                CE = {k: conns(k, "B-a", "W-a", gs) for k in S}
                inc = lambda key: CE[key[0]][0][key[1], key[2]] or (pairs == "b" and CE[key[0]][1][key[1], key[2]])
                rows = [(key, v) for key, v in F6.items() if key[3] == ch and key[4] == how and inc(key)]
                ntot = sum(int(CE[k][0].sum() if pairs == "a" else (CE[k][0] | CE[k][1]).sum()) for k in S)
                dep = [key for key, v in rows if v[3] < 0.10 and v[6] > 0]
                fac = [key for key, v in rows if v[3] < 0.10 and v[6] < 0]
                sig = dep + fac
                diff = [key for key in sig if S[key[0]].shank[key[1]] != S[key[0]].shank[key[2]]]
                pd, pf_ = 100 * len(dep) / ntot, 100 * len(fac) / ntot
                psh = 100 * len(diff) / max(len(sig), 1)
                ok = abs(pd - 12.7) <= 1.27 and abs(pf_ - 10.7) <= 1.07 and abs(psh - 32.2) <= 3.22
                off = np.median([v[7] for key, v in rows if np.isfinite(v[7])])
                print(f"{gs} pairs {pairs}, later {ch}, height {how:2s}: {len(rows)} of {ntot} pairs testable; depression {len(dep)} "
                      f"({pd:.1f}%), facilitation {len(fac)} ({pf_:.1f}%); significant pairs on different shanks {len(diff)} "
                      f"({psh:.1f}%); significant either way {len(sig)} ({100 * len(sig) / ntot:.1f}%); all three within tolerance: {ok}; median of the mean permuted difference {off:.2f}")
# null rate: labels assigned at random to the same numbers of spikes
rng0 = np.random.default_rng(601)
nul = []
for key in [x for x in F6 if x[3] == "x" and x[4] == "i"][::5]:
    k, i, j = key[:3]
    tpre, tpost = S[k].spikes_of(i), S[k].spikes_of(j)
    f, l = pfc2.train_labels(tpre)
    sel = np.flatnonzero(f | l)
    perm = rng0.permutation(sel)
    f2 = np.zeros(len(tpre), bool)
    l2 = np.zeros(len(tpre), bool)
    f2[perm[:f.sum()]] = True
    l2[perm[f.sum():]] = True
    nul.append(pfc2.order_effect(tpre, tpost, f2, l2, rng0, "i", nsur=100, nperm=500)[3] < 0.10)
bt = stats.binomtest(int(np.sum(nul)), len(nul), 0.10)
ci = bt.proportion_ci(0.95)
print(f"null check, labels assigned at random: {np.sum(nul)} of {len(nul)} pairs significant at P < 0.10 "
      f"({100 * np.mean(nul):.1f}%, 95% interval {100 * ci.low:.1f} to {100 * ci.high:.1f}%; expected {0.1 * len(nul):.1f} "
      f"+- {np.sqrt(0.09 * len(nul)):.1f}; binomial test against 10%: p = {bt.pvalue:.2f})")

Result: not reproduced. With the two-sided P taken from both tails of the permutation distribution, depressing pairs are 4.0 to 5.9% and facilitating pairs 5.1 to 10.6% of the connections under G-b (G-a 4.6 to 6.4% and 5.5 to 9.9%), against 12.7% and 10.7%; facilitation is within tolerance under two readings of G-b (10.5% and 10.6%, later spikes as any spike within 40 ms and summed heights) and two of G-a (9.8% and 9.9%), depression under none. 27.3 to 33.3% of the significant pairs are on different shanks (32.2 +- 3.22). On synthetic trains the test finds a fourfold difference in efficacy in 20 of 20 runs, in either direction, and with equal efficacy it flags 3 of 20 runs, all as depression; with labels assigned at random to the data's spikes, 16 of 121 pairs (13.2%, 95% interval 7.8 to 20.6%) are significant at P < 0.10, consistent with the nominal 10% (binomial p = 0.23). The share of connections significant either way, 10.9 to 14.9% under G-b (11.6 to 15.0% under G-a), is at this random-label rate, so the pairs called depressing or facilitating are not more than the test finds by chance, and facilitation within tolerance under two readings is not partial support for the claim.

fig7-supralinear-coincidence¶

Coincident spikes of two or more presynaptic cells within 5 ms discharge their common target interneuron supralinearly, more than the sum of their separate effects, while coincidences in windows over 10 ms add only linearly.

A satellite is a putative interneuron (B-a W-a, C-a) receiving excitatory connections from two or more putative pyramidal cells. An event is a presynaptic spike with k distinct presynaptic cells spiking in the window w ending at it, and no presynaptic spike in the 4 ms after it; it transmits when the target fires 1 to 4 ms after it. p1 is from events with k = 1 (no other presynaptic cell within w before or 4 ms after). Supralinear: (a) p_k > k p1, (b) p_k > 1 - (1 - p1)^k. Events with too few occurrences (under 20) give no value.

In [38]:
def satellite_curve(s, pres, tgt, w):
    tl = [s.spikes_of(p) for p in pres]
    t = np.concatenate(tl)
    c = np.concatenate([np.full(len(x), n) for n, x in enumerate(tl)])
    o = np.argsort(t)
    t, c = t[o], c[o]
    tt = s.spikes_of(tgt)
    nxt = np.append(np.diff(t), np.inf)
    a = np.searchsorted(t, t - w, side="right")
    k = np.array([len(np.unique(c[a[m]:m + 1])) for m in range(len(t))])
    i0 = np.searchsorted(tt, t + 0.001, side="left")
    i1 = np.searchsorted(tt, t + 0.004, side="right")
    hit = i1 > i0
    clean = nxt > 0.004
    prev_other = np.array([np.any(c[a[m]:m] != c[m]) for m in range(len(t))])
    p = {}
    for kk in (1, 2, 3):
        m = clean & (k == kk) & ((~prev_other) if kk == 1 else True)
        p[kk] = (hit[m].mean() if m.sum() >= 20 else np.nan, int(m.sum()))
    return p


def satellites(gs):
    out = []
    for k, s in S.items():
        E, I = conns(k, "B-a", "W-a", gs)
        pyr, inn = TYPES[(k, "B-a", "W-a", "C-a", gs)]
        for tgt in np.flatnonzero(inn):
            pres = np.flatnonzero(E[:, tgt] & pyr)
            if len(pres) >= 2:
                out.append((k, tgt, pres))
    return out


for gs in GS:
    sat = satellites(gs)
    print(f"{gs} B-a W-a: satellites {len(sat)} (paper 14); within 14 +- 1.4: {abs(len(sat) - 14) <= 1.4}; presynaptic cells "
          f"per satellite {[len(x[2]) for x in sat]}")
SAT = satellites("G-b")
print("supralinearity, G-b satellites:")
for w in (0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02):
    rows = []
    for k, tgt, pres in SAT:
        p = satellite_curve(S[k], pres, tgt, w)
        rows.append([p[1][0], p[2][0], p[3][0], p[2][1], p[3][1]])
    R = np.array(rows, float)
    p1, p2, p3 = R[:, 0], R[:, 1], R[:, 2]
    for kk, pk in ((2, p2), (3, p3)):
        ok = ~np.isnan(pk) & ~np.isnan(p1)

        print(f"window {w * 1000:4.0f} ms, k = {kk}: {ok.sum()} satellites with values; mean p{kk} {np.mean(pk[ok]):.3f}, "
              f"mean p1 {np.mean(p1[ok]):.3f}; above k*p1 in {np.sum(ex_a > 0)}, mean excess {np.mean(ex_a):.3f} "
              f"(s.d. {np.std(ex_a, ddof=1) if ok.sum() > 1 else np.nan:.3f}); above 1-(1-p1)^k in {np.sum(ex_b > 0)}, "

Result: not reproduced. The test finds 16 satellites under G-b (15 under G-a, within 14 +- 1.4). With 5 ms windows the mean transmission probability after two coincident presynaptic cells is 0.064 against 0.054 after one, below 2 p1 and 1 - (1 - p1)^2 in all 16 satellites; after three cells (2 satellites with enough events) 0.119 against 0.090, below both predictions. No window from 2 to 20 ms gives a mean above the linear predictions; at 2 ms, 3 of 15 satellites lie above them.

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The data set holds three of the paper's four rats (EE, FF, GG, taken to be the paper's E, F and G; rat H is absent), only correct trials in its trial tables, and, for each session, a selection of the cells (CellsInfo; the files list 1,495 clusters, 627 cells). The layer 5 session of Figure 2a and Supplementary Figure 11 (142 cells) is not in the data set, so every layer 5 value of a single-session claim is untested. Error trials and the individual nose-pokes come from the sensor channels of EE188's .eeg file, so task performance and the sensor-based odor window are for that session only. The number of permutations and surrogates is 1,000 except for the spike-order test (100 surrogates, 500 permutations). The global band of the jitter test follows the Methods' stepping procedure (G-b), with 1% on each side (G-a) as a variant. The detected connections include 41 of the authors' 43 pairs_all for EE188 under G-b B-a W-a (all 43 under G-a B-a W-a, 42 with W-b; 34 under B-b), but the fraction of connected pairs is 1.2 to 1.7 times the paper's under G-b, and the counts that follow from them (cell types, hub, connection probabilities) differ accordingly; with shifted spike trains the detector's false-positive rate is 0.12 to 0.15% (excitatory) and 0.04 to 0.07% (inhibitory) of pairs in EE188.

What was found about the data set. The data description names EE188_example.mat as a file of folder EE0708; it is a member of EE.188.tar.gz. The CellsInfo type column, described as pyramidal, interneuron or unknown, holds no unknown cell in the 12 sessions of behaviors.zip or in EE188_Behavior_PFC.mat (87 and 18 in EE188), while the example file of the same session gives 33, 15 and 69; how either was derived is not documented. EE188_Behavior_PFC.mat holds 105 of the example's 117 cells. The spikes' trial labels and positions run from the first nose-poke, while the description defines the trial start as the end of the nose-poke. The trial table of EE188 leaves out 3 trials that the sensor channels and the position file show as correct; in two of them the rat reaches the arm about 3 minutes after its last poke, longer than any table trial. In 10 of 13 sessions the second LED is not tracked, so head direction is available only in EE152, EE165 and EE188. The layer of each rat is not given in the data set; it comes from the paper's Supplementary Figure 1.
